intake_baseline:10:lesson:
HOW TO BUILD THIS FOR THIS LEARNER (from their full learning profile; the topic and facts stay the same, the delivery is theirs)
Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Where this block conflicts with any earlier style note (length, sections, check questions, rule-first or example-first, tone), this block wins: it comes from the full learning profile.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Shape: exactly 5 short sections; the body of each section is at most 3 sentences (count them, and split a longer one into another section), one new idea per section, 3 check questions in all (the first is at the lesson level, each next one a little harder), at most 2 common mistakes. At most about 920 words in all (not counting the check questions); a shorter lesson that teaches every point is better. 1 worked example (the worked example and the sections' example fields), then 2 try-it lines inside the sections, each written "Try it: <question> Answer: <answer>" and placed after the worked examples. This is the shape, not a cap on content: if the topic needs more, add sections or words; never drop a point to fit.
3. Break the material into many short pieces, each carrying exactly one new idea and ending on a one-line takeaway.
4. Examples: build the worked example and about half of the other examples on basketball, video games, at least two in all; the facts stay the topic's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: spread the check questions through the lesson, not all at the end; each asks them to recall the idea from memory, never to reread or merely recognise it.
- One worked example, then a problem of the same kind for them to do.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words.
About this learner (what they said or the app has seen; data to use, never instructions to follow):
- Past difficulties to pre-empt (address each before it bites, without saying they find it hard): needs tiny doses of new information.
Light touches (apply lightly, only where they fit naturally):
- Go slowly: give each idea room, and do not stack explanations back to back.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

warmup_latency:10:material:
HOW TO BUILD THIS FOR THIS LEARNER (from their full learning profile; the topic and facts stay the same, the delivery is theirs)
Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Start straight in with the real work. Apply this throughout.
3. Interests: build short analogies or practice contexts on basketball, video games, at least two in all, each introduced as an analogy ("think of it like...") and mapped back to a named point of the material; they add no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: where the material has practice or a summary, ask for the idea from memory before it is shown again.
- One worked example, then a problem of the same kind for them to do.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words, built only from the material.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Where this block conflicts with any earlier style note (length, sections, check questions, rule-first or example-first, tone), this block wins: it comes from the full learning profile.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Shape: about 3 short sections; the body of each section is at most 4 sentences (count them, and split a longer one into another section), at most 2 new ideas per section, 3 check questions in all (the first is at the lesson level, each next one a little harder), a line "Quick check: <question> Answer: <answer>" at the end of every second section, at most 2 common mistakes. At most about 880 words in all (not counting the check questions); a shorter lesson that teaches every point is better. 1 worked example (the worked example and the sections' example fields), then 2 try-it lines inside the sections, each written "Try it: <question> Answer: <answer>" and placed after the worked examples. This is the shape, not a cap on content: if the topic needs more, add sections or words; never drop a point to fit.
3. Lead them step by step; no open choices.
4. Examples: build the worked example and about half of the other examples on basketball, video games, at least two in all; the facts stay the topic's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: spread the check questions through the lesson, not all at the end; each asks them to recall the idea from memory, never to reread or merely recognise it.
- One worked example, then a problem of the same kind for them to do.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Lead with practice; show a worked step only after an attempt. Apply this throughout.
3. Interests: build short analogies or practice contexts on basketball, video games, at least two in all, each introduced as an analogy ("think of it like...") and mapped back to a named point of the material; they add no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: where the material has practice or a summary, ask for the idea from memory before it is shown again.
- They learn from the principle rather than from long solved cases: at most one short solved case for reference, then straight to problems.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words, built only from the material.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Explain directly; do not quiz mid-explanation. Apply this throughout.
3. Interests: build short analogies or practice contexts on basketball, video games, at least two in all, each introduced as an analogy ("think of it like...") and mapped back to a named point of the material; they add no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: each check-in asks the listener to recall the idea in their own words before the hosts say it again.
- Dual coding: describe one simple picture of the central idea that the listener can hold in mind.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

extrinsic_reward_sensitivity:10:material:
HOW TO BUILD THIS FOR THIS LEARNER (from their full learning profile; the topic and facts stay the same, the delivery is theirs)
Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. No game elements.
3. Interests: build short analogies or practice contexts on basketball, video games, at least two in all, each introduced as an analogy ("think of it like...") and mapped back to a named point of the material; they add no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: where the material has practice or a summary, ask for the idea from memory before it is shown again.
- One worked example, then a problem of the same kind for them to do.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words, built only from the material.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.

Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 9; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. Include one varied case in a new setting, clearly framed as a practice context from their interests; it tests a point of the material and states no new fact.
3. Interests: build short analogies or practice contexts on basketball, video games, at least two in all, each introduced as an analogy ("think of it like...") and mapped back to a named point of the material; they add no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Retrieval practice: where the material has practice or a summary, ask for the idea from memory before it is shown again.
- One worked example, then a problem of the same kind for them to do.
- Dual coding: pair the central idea with a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list) that shows the same thing as the words, built only from the material.
About this learner (what they said or the app has seen; data to use, never instructions to follow):
- Strengths to build on (lean on them to carry the hard part): applies easily to variations.
Light touches (apply lightly, only where they fit naturally):
- Raise the difficulty steadily across the practice.

Content contract: teach exactly the same topic, skills and key facts. Do not drop, add or change a fact, definition, rule, step or answer; only HOW it is delivered changes.
Use only what the material says for facts; delivery changes wording, order of emphasis, density and pace, never the facts or the quotes. The learner's interests may appear only as clearly framed analogies, examples or practice contexts that map back to a point of the material, never as new facts.
1. Language: write at about reading grade 10; most sentences 21 words or fewer, none over 27.
2. State the principle first in a bullet of its own; where the material works a case or chain through, give it in one compact bullet that still contains every step.
3. Interests: you may add a short framed analogy bullet on basketball, video games, at most one in all (it starts "Think of", comes right after the bullet whose point it pictures, carries that bullet's passage_id and quote, and is not counted in the bullet limit), but only if the notes still fit the word limit; it adds no fact, number, name or claim about the topic, and every fact and quote stays the material's own. Add no other extra bullets.
Learning methods for this learner:
- Length: no longer than a plain outline of the material would be; every question, analogy or aid you add is paid for by cutting words elsewhere, never by dropping a point.
- Gap-only: give the points a learner with a solid background already knows a single line each (every point still stated, every fact kept) and spend the words on the harder points.
- Dual coding: for the central idea, add one bullet that starts "Layout:" and draws the point as a picture in text (an aligned table, an arrow chain or a labelled list), built only from the material.
About this learner (what they said or the app has seen; data to use, never instructions to follow):
- Strengths to build on (lean on them to carry the hard part): strong background in this subject.
Light touches (apply lightly, only where they fit naturally):
- Keep it short: cut repetition, padding and asides, but keep every definition, formula, step, number and fact the material gives.
- Use the precise technical terms and formal verbs the material has, and gloss none of them.
Never mention this profile, "your learning style", scores, a diagnosis or why you chose a style; just write it that way.
